structure.title: 1. FinTech SME Loan Market in France
3. Credit Dynamics (event study, propensity score matching, balance)
3.3 Credit dynamics of FinTech, bank and rejected borrowers (Table 4)
4. Why Does Bank Credit Increase after a FinTech Loan? (collateral channel, alternatives)

observations.statement: The identifying assumption for the matched comparison is stated in the introduction: observably similar FinTech and benchmark borrowers have similar credit demand. The main threat (firms with investment opportunities applying to several lenders at once) is named up front and the two benchmark groups are described as addressing it in complementary ways.
observations.quote: observably similar FinTech and benchmark borrowers have similar credit demand

observations.statement: Each benchmark group is introduced with an explicit strength and limitation: bank borrowers share credit demand and quality but do not use FinTech; rejected applicants share the application decision but may be lower quality. The authors argue that similar results across both benchmarks make unobservables an unlikely driver.

The shift-share IV section spells out relevance and exclusion conditions, names the main threat (collateral requirements correlated with local economic conditions), and says the exclusion restriction cannot be tested formally but is assessed in three ways. A footnote places the design in the exogenous-shifts framework and explains why an exogenous-shares approach does not apply.
observations.quote: we cannot formally test the exclusion restriction assumption

observations.statement: The IV coefficient is explicitly interpreted as a LATE for compliers responding to bank collateral requirements. Because compliers cannot be directly identified, cross-sectional heterogeneity in the first stage (small and low-tangibility firms) is used in an appendix section as a proxy for who they are.
observations.locator: Section 4.3.2, footnote 44, Internet Appendix Section I

observations.statement: A footnote addresses a possible correlation between collateral requirements and bank credit supply by arguing in which direction it would bias the first and second stages, and states that a shift-share credit supply control is added anyway.

Data sources are listed one by one in numbered subsections (scraped aggregator website, central bank FinTech reporting, credit registry, loan-level bank survey, FIBEN/Orbis firm financials, bankruptcy bulletin) and linked through a unique firm identifier. A variable dictionary is placed in an Internet Appendix table.

Platform exclusions (equity or bond platforms, an agriculture-only platform) are justified by comparability with bank loans, with each excluded platform and its market share listed in a footnote. The sample end date is justified by the need for a post-origination window and by avoiding the pandemic period, which is documented in an appendix section.

The unmatched sample is built as an ordered list: industry exclusions, minimum presence in the credit registry before the event, a definition of new relationship loans, restriction to fixed-term bank loans (excluding revolving, working capital and leasing loans for comparability with unsecured FinTech loans), one event per firm chosen at random, and exclusion of the new loan from the outcome.
Two Internet Appendix tables document, for every table and figure, the sample restrictions, frequency, time period, event window and number of firms by group.

Because the collateral field in the loan-level survey exists only from a given quarter, tests relying on collateral (including the shift-share analysis) use a later sample start than the main analysis; the paper states this explicitly and table notes restate the period per table.

When the matched sample is linked to the loan-level survey, the loss of firms (concentrated among rejected applicants) is acknowledged in a footnote, and the authors state they therefore focus on the bank-borrower benchmark for that test.

The main outcome is the log of total outstanding bank credit at the firm-month level, excluding the new relationship loan. For the lender-type split only, log(1+x) is used so that the outcome is defined for new lenders, and this exception is flagged in a footnote.

Treatment status is a firm-level indicator for having obtained a FinTech loan versus belonging to a benchmark group; the event date is the origination or rejection date, and the post indicator switches on at relative month zero.

The instrument is built in two displayed steps: a bank-quarter secured ratio (count-based, justified in a footnote as more representative of small loans) and a firm-level weighted average using credit shares lagged two quarters. The lag is justified by possible endogenous response of exposure to tightening requirements.
Firm outcomes are log-transformed except working capital, which can be negative and is instead scaled by lagged total assets; the choice is explained in the text.

The collateral outcome is an indicator for pledging specific assets in a quarter, with zero assigned both to unsecured loans and to quarters with no sampled loan. A footnote cautions that coefficients measure the probability of obtaining a secured loan from a reporting branch, not from any bank.

The main table reports two fixed effect structures side by side for each benchmark (firm-year versus firm plus month), with FE rows, N and R-squared, and notes restating the equation, the sample window and the cluster level. The text explains why the firm-year version is chosen as baseline.

Every regression table prints the estimating equation in its notes, restates the definitions of Post and the outcome, names the benchmark group per panel, and repeats the sample period and clustering. Tables are organised as Panel A (bank benchmark) and Panel B (rejected benchmark) with identical column layouts.

The IV table follows an OLS, first stage, reduced form, IV column order, labels the sample per column (unmatched versus shift-share), lists firm controls and the credit-supply control as rows, and adds rows for the robust first-stage F statistic and two weak-IV-robust confidence intervals.

Matching is described as five nearest neighbours with replacement, and the text notes that a benchmark firm can be matched to several treated firms; however, no regression weights are mentioned in the text or in table notes.
observations.note: Weights are absent from the paper's description; see concordance.

observations.statement: Standard errors are clustered at the firm level throughout (stated in text and in every table and figure note), but the paper gives no explicit reason for choosing this level. The descriptive loan comparison table clusters by industry instead, also without justification.

Following a cited guide on IV in corporate finance, the paper reports the Kleibergen-Paap robust F statistic against the conventional threshold and adds Anderson-Rubin and Lee et al. tF-type confidence intervals so that inference remains valid under weak instruments.
observations.locator: Table 8 Panel A bottom rows, Section 4.3.2

observations.statement: Balance is shown twice: a four-panel table of means, differences and t statistics before and after matching for both benchmark groups, and a coefficient plot of standardized differences with confidence intervals. Remaining imbalances are discussed with their sign relative to the hypothesis.
observations.locator: Table 3 Panels A to D, Figure 2, Section 3.2.3

observations.statement: Pre-trends are inspected visually in raw form (log credit paths for matched groups in an appendix figure) and in regression form (monthly event-study coefficients with confidence intervals relative to month minus one in the main text). A credit-line utilisation series is also plotted in an appendix as a direct demand proxy.
observations.locator: Figure 3, Internet Appendix Figures C.1 and C.2

observations.statement: The first stage is reported as a full column of the main IV table, interpreted in the text in standard deviation units, and its strength is compared across the placebo lagged-shift columns using the robust F statistic.

Two placebo designs support the exclusion restriction: replacing the contemporaneous shift with shifts lagged two to five quarters (expected to fail if local conditions drive results), and replacing the collateral-intensive outcome with other loan types (expected to be null under the collateral channel).

The stability of the shares is checked in an appendix table by rebuilding the instrument with shares lagged three or four quarters, interpreted as evidence that shifts rather than shares drive the variation.

Robustness of the matched DiD is delegated to an appendix section: alternative matching procedures (one nearest neighbour with and without replacement), dropping the two platforms with larger loans, dropping firms with missing characteristics, and running on the unmatched sample. Results are summarised in one sentence as quantitatively similar.
observations.locator: Section 3.3 last paragraph, Internet Appendix Section D

observations.statement: A footnote explains why event-study coefficients are identified outside the treatment year with firm fixed effects and points to an appendix figure showing dynamic coefficients under both fixed-effect structures.
IV robustness adds quarter fixed effects interacted with industry, region, rating or size (appendix table), and the placebo columns are placed in the main table's Panel B rather than in the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 4.3.3, Table 8 Panel B, Internet Appendix Table I.1

observations.statement: To rule out that unsecured bank loans would produce the same effect, an appendix figure restricts benchmark bank borrowers to those whose new loan is not secured on specific assets.
The speed-based alternative is addressed by removing early repayers, with the check stated in a footnote and in the text rather than in a table.

Heterogeneity is always run as split samples (loan purpose, rated versus unrated, high versus low interest rate), and the propensity score matching is re-run within each subsample so that treated and benchmark firms are matched on the same split. A footnote notes that rejected applicants cannot be split by purpose and only their matched counterparts are retained.

Outcome-side splits (long-term versus other loans; existing versus new lenders; local versus distant lenders) are used as heterogeneity by decomposing the dependent variable rather than the sample, with the split definitions tied to cited literature on information asymmetry.

The mechanism section derives three testable predictions from the collateral channel and tests each in turn (credit product, loan purpose, direct collateral pledging), then confronts two named alternatives (information, speed) with predictions that go the opposite way, and closes with a summary paragraph stating all predictions are verified.

Firm-level uses of funds (assets, tangible assets, employment, working capital components) are examined as intermediate outcomes, and the interpretation of the Post versus interaction coefficients is spelled out by construction of the two benchmarks.

A footnote uses loan-to-value reasoning to distinguish sequential from simultaneous financing and compares implied multipliers from OLS and IV, while stating the paper does not formally distinguish the two.

Percent effects are converted into euro amounts for the median firm (median chosen over mean because credit is skewed, explained in a footnote), and these amounts are compared across outcomes (extra bank credit versus reduction in payables) and with the size of the FinTech loan.
observations.locator: footnote 45, Section 5.1, Internet Appendix Section J

observations.statement: The first stage is interpreted per standard deviation of the instrument and relative to the unconditional mean; the IV-OLS gap is discussed via LATE and measurement error (with a citation), and the IV estimate is turned into euros of bank credit per euro of FinTech funding for proxy complier groups.

Interest-expense and investor-return calculations combine regression estimates with summary statistics and external parameters from cited studies (trade credit cost, corporate bond yields); details are placed in appendix sections and the break-even assumption is made explicit.
observations.locator: Section 5.2, footnote 46, Internet Appendix Sections J and K

observations.statement: A binned scatter of new loan size against subsequent bank credit growth for the two groups is used to compare fitted slopes, with slope coefficients and significance printed on the figure.

Limits of the collateral data are stated in footnotes: only pledges of specific assets are observed, not personal guarantees or cash collateral, and secured status is observed only for loans sampled by reporting branches.

A mechanical reduction in drawn credit lines for FinTech borrowers caused by the sample construction is explained in a long footnote, together with a check excluding used credit lines from the other-loans outcome.

Results for the rejected-applicant benchmark in the collateral pledging test are explicitly flagged as to be read with the caveat of sample loss; the negative Post coefficient is given a tentative interpretation with a citation.

The conclusion has a dedicated generalisation paragraph arguing portability beyond France (collateral constraints are widespread; FinTech loans are typically unsecured elsewhere, supported by surveys and platform websites), and separately flags unbanked firms and other channels as open questions.

Figures are event-study coefficient plots with confidence intervals (base period minus one), a standardized-difference balance plot, and one binned scatter. Tables use three-level stars, standard errors in parentheses, and notes that restate the equation, sample window and clustering. Descriptive statistics appear in two main-text tables and appendix figures.

Internet Appendix material is referenced by lettered sections and tables or figures (A.1 to K), covering variable definitions, sample descriptions, robustness, heterogeneity in the first stage, and calculations; the appendix is hosted separately by the publisher and is not part of the read text.

The introduction previews every result in the order of the paper (credit dynamics, mechanism, IV, overborrowing), followed by four literature-contribution paragraphs. The body goes institutional background, data, event study and matched DiD, mechanisms with an embedded IV, then real outcomes and defaults, then conclusion.

There is no roadmap paragraph and no separate robustness section; robustness is folded into the end of each results subsection with pointers to appendix sections. Hypotheses are stated as numbered testable predictions before the tests.

The IV is introduced after the mechanism evidence and framed as building on it (firms exploit the unsecured nature of FinTech loans), rather than as the primary identification; the text says matched comparisons are the main strategy.

A one-sentence Code Availability statement at the end of the conclusion points to a Harvard Dataverse DOI for the replication code. No data availability statement or software is mentioned in the text.

Data combine central bank administrative and confidential registry files, a web-scraped aggregator, a commercial firm database, a public bankruptcy bulletin and a proprietary rejected-applicant list shared by one platform (acknowledged by name). No access procedure is described.

Before the main analysis, FinTech and bank loans are compared by regressing loan size, maturity and rate on a FinTech indicator with progressive fixed effects, and firms are compared with proxies for financing constraints chosen with citations to the literature.

Two benchmark groups: matched bank borrowers and matched rejected FinTech applicants.
IV stages include the matching covariates as controls plus a shift-share credit supply control.

Alternative matching, platform exclusions, alternative fixed effects, lagged shares, interacted time fixed effects.
Ten main tables and six figures plus lettered Internet Appendix material.

gaps: No justification for clustering at the firm level (or by industry in Table 2).
No data availability statement or access procedure for the confidential registry and survey data.
No software or package named in the text.
No formal pre-trend test statistic; pre-trends are assessed visually from coefficient plots.
No mean of the dependent variable reported in regression tables.
No discussion of multiple testing across the many split-sample tables.
Regression weights used in the code are not described in the paper.
Internet Appendix is not included in the text file, so appendix practices are recorded only from main-text pointers.

reading.note: All 51 pages read, including references (pages 48 to 51). The Internet Appendix (sections A to K) is a separate publisher file and is not part of the text; its contents are recorded only as cited from the main text.
